query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A pre-oxidation treatment that forms a thin, adherent and nanocrystalline oxide layer on the FeNiCrCoCu coating improves high‐temperature wear resistance by reducing microscale plastic deformation during sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: A sputtered or deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating in the as-deposited (minimal surface oxidation) condition on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled pre-oxidation treatment, performed at a temperature close to the operating regime (e.g., around or slightly below 600°C) in a low-to-moderate oxygen partial pressure environment to deliberately form a thin, continuous oxide layer on the coating surface.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear tests conducted above 600°C in atmospheres with controlled oxygen content (operating conditions typical for the intended high-temperature application).
generation.structural_mediator: A nanocrystalline, protective oxide layer that forms on the surface.
generation.mechanism: The deliberately formed oxide layer acts as a barrier that both reduces the intensity of direct metal-to-metal contact during sliding and limits the development of subsurface plastic deformation. This modification shifts the dominant wear mechanism from severe plastic deformation and adhesive wear to more benign oxidative wear, thereby enhancing overall wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as-deposited coating, the pre-oxidized coating will exhibit a lower coefficient of friction, reduced wear rate (i.e., lower material loss), and less evidence of localized plastic deformation or microstructural damage under sliding conditions at >600°C.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating with minimal pre-formed oxide.
generation.boundary: This improvement in wear resistance is expected only under high-temperature conditions (e.g., >600°C) in controlled oxygen environments that allow formation and stability of the protective oxide layer; at lower temperatures or in oxygen-poor conditions the effect may not manifest.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain how exactly the specific oxide composition on a FeNiCrCoCu alloy will form or evolve under identical pre-oxidation conditions, and whether any adverse effects (e.g., oxide layer spallation or brittleness) could counteract the beneficial effects at extreme stress conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coated samples on the same substrate: one group with the controlled pre-oxidation treatment to form a thin oxide layer and a control group with the as-deposited (minimal oxide) condition. Subject both groups to identical high-temperature sliding wear tests (e.g., at 650-700°C) under controlled oxygen partial pressures.
measurements: Wear rate (material loss quantified by weight loss or wear track volume)
Microscopic evaluation of deformation (e.g., via SEM, TEM) in the near-surface region
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in friction and wear rate, or if microscopic analysis reveals equal or greater subsurface plastic deformation compared to the baseline as-deposited samples, the hypothesis that the controlled oxide layer improves wear resistance by mediating deformation would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . occupying_moves.conditions: Test coatings at operating temperatures (e.g., >600°C) under controlled oxygen partial pressures comparing baseline (minimal pre-oxidation) versus coatings with an induced thin oxide layer

chosen.technique: in situ high-temperature tribometer tests with a pre-oxidation treatment protocol
chosen.conditions: Sliding wear experiments performed above 600°C in atmospheres with controlled oxygen content to promote a thin, protective oxide layer relative to a baseline as-deposited coating
chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by testing the hypothesis that an in situ formed, controlled oxide layer governs microscopic deformation and overall wear. By deliberately pre-oxidizing the coating to generate a nanocrystalline oxide-induced surface modification, the study can compare directional changes in wear resistance and deformation against the baseline. This experiment builds on prior evidence of oxidation-induced surface strengthening in high-temperature conditions, and a lack of correlation between the induced oxide layer and improved wear resistance would falsify the hypothesis.
